strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practical problem: efficient RoI identification for fine-grained perception in MLLMs, clearly articulating the trade-off between training-based (data-hungry) and training-free (slow, multi-pass) approaches.

The self-distillation idea is cleanly executed: denoising internal attention maps (sink-token removal based on feature norms, selective binary label assignment with an ignored ambiguous region) to produce sparse pseudo-labels is a sensible and well-justified pipeline, supported by an empirical analysis (Fig. 3) of attention-vs-localization behavior.

The efficiency argument is convincing: the RPN operates on middle-layer features with a single partial forward pass, decoupled from auto-regressive decoding, yielding 1.5x faster RoI prediction than ViCrop and better throughput (0.62x vs 0.42x) with higher accuracy.

Evaluation is broad: four MLLMs across two families (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL 1.3B/7B), nine benchmarks, unified lmms-eval protocol, and thorough ablations covering backbone depth (B), RPN depth (R), training-set size, pseudo-label source (self vs. GT responses), and pre/post-smoothing.

The counter-intuitive finding that self-generated responses yield better supervision than ground-truth responses (Tab. 4b) is interesting and backed by a plausible representational-consistency argument plus a theoretical motivation in Appendix E.
Reproducibility is strong: full training hyperparameters, per-model layer configurations, complete training algorithm pseudocode, prompts, and stated code release.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core recipe—distilling internal attention into a lightweight localization head—closely builds on existing ideas (ViCrop, TwigVLM, attention-based grounding from Kang et al.), and the denoising steps are relatively simple heuristics. The theoretical analysis in Appendix E is a standard MSE decomposition that adds limited insight.

Baseline coverage is narrow. Comparisons are limited to S2 (full tuning) and ViCrop (training-free); several directly relevant training-based RoI methods (V* / SEAL, Visual CoT, DyFo, DeepEyes) are cited but not compared. The exclusion of ViCrop's cropping strategy on V* Bench raises fairness questions about that comparison.

Potential tuning on evaluation data: the label-assignment thresholds (0.2/0.1) are 'empirically set' based on an analysis of a TextVQA subset (Fig. 3), which is also a reported benchmark; layer selections (Table 6) are also chosen empirically per model. This blurs the train/test separation and inflates the reported gains.

The abstract's claim of training on 'only a few (e.g., 10K)' pairs is somewhat misleading—the best main results use the full 152K training set, and the 10K result is only shown in an ablation with notably lower average performance (60.6 vs 62.6).
Only older MLLM families (LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL) are tested; generalization to modern natively high-resolution models (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL) is untested, weakening the practical significance claim.

Some results are marginal or inconsistent: POPE improvements are within ~1 point, InfoVQA gains are small for LLaVA, and throughput numbers fluctuate non-monotonically across configurations without a fully convincing explanation; the text also contains minor internal inconsistencies (e.g., ablation narrative vs. Sec. 3.4 about which upscaling is preferred).

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: efficient, annotation-free RoI identification that avoids multi-pass prefill and auto-regressive decoding, which is a genuine pain point in high-resolution MLLM perception.

Comprehensive ablation studies (raw attention vs. attention prediction vs. label assignment vs. sink-token removal; backbone depth B, RPN depth R, data size, pseudo-label source, pre- vs. post-smoothing) that carefully dissect each component of the pipeline.

Results are reported across two model families (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL 1.3B/7B) and two benchmark categories, with throughput measured on the same hardware and all baselines re-implemented in lmms-eval, which supports fair comparison.

An interesting empirical finding that self-generated responses yield better pseudo-labels than ground-truth SFT responses, with a plausible 'representational consistency' explanation; the data-efficiency analysis (10K samples already gives large gains) is valuable.
A concrete Algorithm 1, hyperparameter tables, and layer-selection rationale improve reproducibility relative to typical submissions.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and significant overlap with prior work: middle-layer attention for grounding is already established (Kang et al., 2025), weight-initialization from pretrained MLLM layers and the overall RPN-on-frozen-backbone design closely follow TwigVLM (Shao et al., 2025, whose hyperparameters are even adopted), and ViCrop already established the two-stage crop paradigm. The core contribution reduces to a denoising/thresholding pipeline (sink-token removal + confidence thresholds + ignore regions) that is largely engineering.

Missing baselines and incomplete evaluation: comparisons are limited to S2 and ViCrop; recent training-based and RL-based RoI methods (e.g., DeepEyes, VILA-HD-style approaches) are discussed but not compared. No general VQA benchmarks (e.g., MMBench, GQA, MME) are reported to verify the method does not regress broad capabilities; only POPE is included. The statement that ViCrop's cropping strategy 'was not used' on V* Bench makes the head-to-head comparison on that benchmark opaque.

Claim inflation: the abstract emphasizes training on 'only a few (e.g., 10K)' pairs, but all main results use 152K samples; Table 4b shows the 10K setting is meaningfully weaker than the full setting. The abstract's 'over 10% absolute improvement' framing (e.g., +12.6 TextVQA, +17.2 V*) is driven by a very low LLaVA-1.5 baseline and is not representative of the average gains (~7% on text-rich tasks), and some per-benchmark gains are marginal (InfoVQA +1.6, ChartQA +2.0).

Unclear or missing details undermine rigor: the norm threshold τnorm used for sink-token removal is not specified in the main text; no variance over seeds is reported for any result; the code link in the abstract is empty; several inconsistencies between the abstract and results; typos and writing issues ('Gerneration', 'exsiting', 'a empirical', 'initilized') persist.

The theoretical appendix (Appendix E) is basic: the result that regressing a noisy target learns a conditional expectation with lower MSE than the raw noisy signal is a straightforward consequence of standard statistics (variance decomposition), and the assumptions (CCN, additive activation) are unvalidated for real attention maps; it does not materially justify the specific heuristic label-assignment design.

The efficiency argument is weakened by the fact that pseudo-label generation requires full auto-regressive decoding of the frozen MLLM for the entire 152K training set at training time, so the method is not truly 'training-light'; training-time cost is only characterized via a single throughput number (two hours on 4x A6000), and the throughput figures (0.4x-0.6x of baseline) show the method is still substantially slower than the baseline at inference.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem setting: the paper identifies a genuine trade-off between annotation-heavy training-based RoI methods and inefficient training-free attention-based methods, and positions SD-RPN as resolving it via an efficient single-pass, annotation-free design.

Strong empirical results: consistent absolute gains (5-10%+) across four model backbones (LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, DeepSeek-VL-1.3B/7B) and two benchmark families (Document/OCR and vision-centric/high-resolution), demonstrating the approach is not tied to one architecture.

Comprehensive and honest ablations: the study dissects pseudo-label denoising (sink-token removal, selective label assignment), backbone depth (B15R3 sweet spot), RPN depth, data efficiency (even 10K samples give large gains), smoothing strategy, and an instructive negative result showing GT-response pseudo-labels underperform self-generated ones, with a plausible 'representational consistency' explanation.

Good efficiency reporting: throughput is measured relative to the baseline on the same hardware, and the RPN's partial forward-pass design (1.5x faster RoI stage than ViCrop) is a concrete efficiency contribution.

Useful supporting material: Algorithm 1 gives a fully reproducible training specification, Appendix E provides a (albeit standard) theoretical justification for predicting RoI labels over thresholding raw attention, and the LLM-usage disclosure is transparent.
weaknesses: Limited baseline coverage: comparisons are restricted to S2 and ViCrop. Several closely related and recent RoI/visual-search methods (e.g., Deepeyes, ZoomEye-style approaches, V*-based search pipelines, SEAL, or TwigVLM which the hyperparameters were borrowed from) are discussed in related work but not compared against, making it hard to judge state-of-the-art standing.

Overclaiming in abstract/intro: the paper headlines training on 'a few (e.g., 10K)' pairs, but peak reported performance (62.6% avg) requires the full 152K dataset; the 10K setting reaches 60.6%. The headline framing slightly overstates the data-efficiency story relative to the default configuration.

Novelty is moderate: self-distillation from internal MLLM attention, sink-token removal, and middle-layer attention for grounding all build directly on existing analyses (Kang et al. 2025a/b, Darcet et al. 2023, ViCrop, TwigVLM). The core contribution is a careful engineering combination (denoising pipeline + lightweight RPN init) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; Appendix E's theory is a standard conditional-expectation/noise-robustness argument.

Cost asymmetry is underexplored: pseudo-label generation requires full auto-regressive decoding with the frozen MLLM on 152K samples (the very bottleneck the method criticizes in training-free approaches), and throughput still drops to 0.40-0.62x at inference; the paper does not report total end-to-end training cost versus, e.g., simply fine-tuning with S2.

Some fairness and robustness questions: hyperparameters (attention layers, frozen depth B) are tuned per model; a special note that ViCrop's cropping was not used in the V* comparison raises questions about exact comparability; POPE gains are marginal and a few cells degrade (e.g., HR-Bench 8K FCP).

Presentation issues: the code link in the abstract is empty ('Code is available at .'), there are multiple typos ('exsiting', 'Gerneration', 'a empirical'), and inconsistencies such as ablation #5 adopting 'Masked Upscaling' as default while Table 1/2 results appear to use the box-upscaling setting need clarification.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: identifying RoIs efficiently without annotations or multi-pass/auto-regressive overhead, with the RPN operating on middle-layer features in a single partial forward pass.

Comprehensive evaluation across three MLLM families (LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL, Qwen2.5-VL) at multiple scales, covering document/OCR, vision-centric, and high-resolution benchmarks, with re-implemented baselines in lmms-eval for fairness.

Thorough ablation studies that systematically validate each design choice (pseudo-label denoising, label assignment, sink-token removal, backbone depth B, RPN depth R, training data size, thresholds, smoothing strategy), including a useful counter-intuitive finding that self-generated responses yield better pseudo-labels than ground-truth responses.

Beyond headline numbers, the paper includes meaningful efficiency analyses: throughput trade-offs, comparison against naive resolution scaling (Fig. 6), and a practical comparison to external grounding models (Grounding-DINO) that quantifies both latency and accuracy advantages.

Detailed algorithmic specification (Algorithm 1), hyperparameters, layer selection rationale, failure case analysis, and a theoretical appendix explaining why learned predictors of attention outperform raw attention thresholds, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate/incremental: combining noisy internal attention with denoising heuristics (norm-based sink removal, confidence thresholds, minimal bounding box) and distilling into a lightweight RPN is an engineering contribution; closely related ideas exist in ViCrop, TwigVLM, attention-sink literature, and self-distillation works, and the paper does not sharply delineate what is fundamentally new beyond assembling these components.

Some claims appear overstated relative to evidence: the abstract emphasizes training on 'only a few (e.g., 10K)' samples and 'over 10% absolute accuracy improvement', but the best results use 152K samples, and the 10% figure is cherry-picked for specific benchmarks/models while average gains are ~3-9%.

The efficiency story is undercut by the reported throughput (0.40x-0.62x of baseline): the method trades substantial compute for accuracy like the two-stage baselines it criticizes, and end-to-end throughput comparisons with ViCrop are confined to a single claim (1.5x faster RoI stage) rather than a complete latency breakdown.

Baselines are uneven across model families: S2/ViCrop comparisons are only for LLaVA-1.5; for DeepSeek-VL there are no crop-based baselines at all, making it hard to attribute the large gains specifically to SD-RPN versus the two-stage paradigm generally.

Presentation issues reduce polish: broken code link ('Code is available at .'), typos ('exsiting', 'Gerneration', 'vision-centriand', 'Data Efficency'), and some improvement annotations in Table 2 that appear inconsistent with the tabulated values.

The pseudo-label pipeline introduces several hand-tuned hyperparameters (tau_norm, tau_fg, tau_bg, Gaussian filter, binarization threshold) whose generalization across future models is unclear, and the theoretical appendix (Appendix F) is largely a restatement of standard regression-under-noise results rather than a substantive analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and timely problem (efficient RoI identification for fine-grained MLLM perception) and the proposed solution is sensible: a lightweight RPN attached to frozen middle layers, trained with denoised attention-derived pseudo-labels, avoiding both annotated data and multi-pass/auto-regressive RoI prediction.

Evaluation breadth is above average: the method is applied to three MLLM families (LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL, Qwen2.5-VL) at multiple scales, across ten benchmarks, with re-implemented baselines in a unified eval library (lmms-eval).

Extensive ablations: pseudo-label components (label assignment, sink-token removal), backbone depth, RPN depth, thresholds, smoothing, data size, and comparisons to alternative supervision (GT responses, MSE regression, external Grounding-DINO), plus failure-case analysis.

Data efficiency is genuinely demonstrated (10K samples already yield most of the gain), and the counter-intuitive finding that self-generated responses yield better distillation targets than GT responses is an interesting empirical observation.

Appendices include the full training algorithm, hyperparameters, and layer-selection details, which supports reproducibility, and a theoretical motivation (Appendix F) for why regressing on attention beats thresholding raw attention.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core insight—that middle-layer response-to-image attention contains grounding signal (Kang et al., 2025b) and can supervise a lightweight RoI head—is incremental. The pseudo-label 'denoising pipeline' is essentially heuristic thresholding (norm-based sink removal, relative-attention cutoffs, minimal bounding box), which is straightforward engineering rather than a deep methodological contribution. The theory in Appendix F is standard noise-model/conditional-expectation material dressed up as support for the design.

Claims are stronger than the evidence. The abstract states training uses 'a few (e.g., 10K)' samples and claims '>10% absolute accuracy improvement' on TextVQA, DocVQA, and V-Star, but the main results (Tabs. 1–2) use the full 152K dataset and the average gains are ~7% on Doc/OCR and ~3% over the already-strong Qwen2.5-VL baseline. Cherry-picking the best-case improvements in the abstract is misleading.

Inconsistencies across the manuscript raise correctness concerns: Table 11 reports DeepSeek-VL + SD-RPN DocVQA at 64.5 while Table 1 reports 67.2; Table 11 contains apparent typos ('456*' for Mini-Gemini OCRBench, ChartQA for DeepSeek-VL missing from Table 1); there are numerous typos throughout ('vision-centriand', 'Gerneration', 'exsiting', 'Data Efficency', 'a empirical'), suggesting insufficient polish for a submission at this stage.

Missing key baselines weaken the central claims. The comparison against ViCrop/S2 is fair, but there is no control for the simplest alternative: standard supervised fine-tuning (or SFT with high-resolution training) on the same 152K samples, which is needed to show the RPN approach beats just training on data; nor a random-crop/center-crop baseline to isolate the benefit of learned RoI prediction from simply appending extra visual tokens. The Grounding-DINO comparison omits the referenced YOLO-World.

Efficiency gains are qualified. Throughput drops to 0.4–0.62x of the baseline in Table 1, and the claimed '1.5x faster than ViCrop' and '20x faster than Grounding-DINO' refer only to the RoI prediction sub-step, while the two-stage pipeline's overall cost (second-stage high-res encoding plus more visual tokens) dominates end-to-end latency; the net efficiency story is less compelling than the framing suggests.

Robustness of results is not established: no error bars, seeds, or variance estimates across runs, and ablation differences (e.g., Table 4a peak at B15R3 vs. B18R3, Table 5 threshold sensitivity, where swapping tau_bg from 0.10 to 0.05 changes the 'default') are within ranges that could plausibly be noise given single-run evaluation.

Some design choices appear under-motivated: layer selection is per-model and 'empirically chosen' (Table 7), the Figure 3 empirical motivation is derived only from TextVQA, and the masked vs. box upscaling analysis is thin. The gains on POPE are marginal or negative in several settings, and the method's dependence on the quality of the base model's own attention is not analyzed in failure regimes beyond anecdote.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem (efficient RoI identification for fine-grained MLLM perception) with a well-motivated solution that avoids both large-scale annotated data and slow multi-pass/auto-regressive localization.

The pseudo-label denoising pipeline (sink-token removal via feature norms + selective binary label assignment with ignored ambiguous tokens) is a sensible and empirically validated design; Fig. 3 and the ablation in Tab. 3 (raw attention 3.8% vs. full pipeline 9.2% avg. gain) convincingly support the central claim that noisy attention is a poor supervision signal.

Broad and fairly strong evaluation: three MLLM families (LLaVA-1.5, DeepSeek-VL, Qwen2.5-VL) across ~9 benchmarks, with re-implemented baselines in a unified eval library, throughput measurements, and a performance-throughput trade-off analysis (Fig. 6) showing superiority over naive resolution scaling.

Thorough ablations: backbone depth (B), RPN depth (R), training data size, pseudo-label thresholds, smoothing placement, plus a counter-intuitive and interesting finding that self-generated responses yield better pseudo-labels than ground-truth responses (Tab. 4b), with a reasonable 'representational consistency' explanation.

Additional valuable analyses: comparison against external grounding models (Grounding-DINO, Tab. 10), taxonomy of attention noise sources (Appendix C.3), failure-case analysis (Fig. 9), and a (somewhat simple but consistent) theoretical justification in Appendix F. Good reproducibility signals: algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameters, prompts, and a stated code release.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core recipe (distill attention-derived RoI supervision into a lightweight head attached to frozen middle layers) closely resembles TwigVLM (Shao et al., 2025), whose training hyperparameters the authors themselves adopt; the delta is essentially the pseudo-label denoising/label-assignment pipeline, which is heuristic and relies on multiple manually tuned thresholds (τnorm, τfg, τbg, τ) with an extensive but post-hoc search (Tab. 5).

The overall pipeline involves many hand-designed heuristics (norm-based sink removal, Gaussian post-smoothing, connected components, box vs. masked upscaling), which raises robustness and generalization concerns; the theoretical appendix proves a fairly trivial point (regression to a noisy target learns its conditional expectation) and does not actually justify the specific label-assignment heuristic.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the abstract headline of '10K samples' contrasts with the main results that use 152K samples; the biggest gains come from the weakest baselines (LLaVA-1.5: +7-9% avg.) while gains shrink substantially on the strongest model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B: ~+3% avg.), suggesting part of the improvement may stem from compensating for weak base-model resolution handling rather than a general mechanism.

Baseline coverage has gaps: no comparison against several relevant recent RoI/zooming approaches (e.g., VILA-HD, ZoomEye, VisPruner, or other V*-style search methods) beyond S2/ViCrop/DeepEyes/Thyme; the ViCrop comparison on V* is also run with its cropping strategy 'disabled', which complicates interpretation; throughput is still 0.4-0.6x of the baseline, so the method trades significant latency for accuracy like its competitors.

Consistency and polish issues undermine confidence: internal inconsistencies (ablation tables appear to use the older threshold defaults even after Tab. 5 establishes a better default, so headline numbers may be understated or inconsistent across sections; Tab. 4a/4b rows with identical averages), several typos ('exsiting', 'Gerneration', 'centriand', 'empirical' phrasing), and a placeholder for the code URL in the abstract.

The evaluation primarily uses accuracy benchmarks; there is no direct quantitative evaluation of RoI localization quality against ground-truth boxes (only a coarse histogram analysis in Fig. 3), which would more directly validate the central claim of 'more precise localization'.
